USERRA — MILITARY LEAVE AND REEMPLOYMENT RIGHTS INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

MILITARY SERVICE / LEAVE DECLARATION
Jordan Lee is providing this information to Acme, Inc. in connection with a period of service in the uniformed services.

Branch/component of service: _______________________________________________
Date service begins (or began): October 1, 2026
Expected or actual date service ends: April 1, 2027
Date advance notice of this service was given to Acme, Inc. (written or verbal), if applicable: _______________________________________________
Cumulative service time with Acme, Inc. to date, including this period (if known): _______________________________________________

RIGHT TO REEMPLOYMENT AFTER SERVICE
Under the federal Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act (USERRA), Jordan Lee is entitled to reemployment with Acme, Inc. after a period of service in the uniformed services if: advance written or verbal notice of the service was given to Acme, Inc. (unless notice was precluded by military necessity or was otherwise impossible or unreasonable); the cumulative length of this and all previous service-related absences from employment with Acme, Inc. does not exceed five years (subject to statutory exceptions to that cap); and Jordan Lee reports back to work or applies for reemployment within the time limits the statute sets, which vary by the length of the service period. This reemployment right also depends on the character of Jordan Lee's discharge from the uniformed service not being dishonorable, bad-conduct, or under other-than-honorable conditions.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "any person whose absence from a position of employment is necessitated by reason of service in the uniformed services shall be entitled to the reemployment rights and benefits and other employment benefits of this chapter if— (1) the person (or an appropriate officer of the uniformed service in which such service is performed) has given advance written or verbal notice of such service to such person’s employer; (2) the cumulative length of the absence and of all previous absences from a position of employment with that employer by reason of service in the uniformed services does not exceed five years; and (3) except as provided in subsection (f), the person reports to, or submits an application for reemployment to, such employer in accordance with the provisions of subsection (e)."
  — 38 U.S.C. § 4312(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, USERRA reemployment rights (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/38/4312)
  "A person’s entitlement to the benefits of this chapter by reason of the service of such person in one of the uniformed services terminates upon the occurrence of any of the following events: (1) A separation of such person from such uniformed service with a dishonorable or bad conduct discharge. (2) A separation of such person from such uniformed service under other than honorable conditions, as characterized pursuant to regulations"
  — 38 U.S.C. § 4304 (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, USERRA character-of-service disqualification (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/38/4304)
  Known gap: This clause states the conditions for entitlement to reemployment; it doesn't determine whether a particular employee's notice, service length, or application timing actually satisfies them. The five-year cumulative service cap has several statutory exceptions not restated here (for example, service required beyond five years to complete an initial period of obligated service, or an inability to obtain release orders through no fault of the service member). Separately, an employer isn't required to reemploy someone under this law if the employer's circumstances have so changed that reemployment is impossible or unreasonable, if reemployment would impose an undue hardship in certain accommodation situations, or if the pre-service job was for a brief, nonrecurrent period with no reasonable expectation of continuing — and the employer bears the burden of proving any of those exceptions applies. This document doesn't resolve whether any of those exceptions apply to a given situation.

THE REEMPLOYMENT POSITION — THE "ESCALATOR PRINCIPLE"
USERRA doesn't simply return a reemployed person to the job they had before their service began. Under 38 U.S.C. § 4313, a person whose service lasted less than 91 days is generally reemployed in the position they would have been employed in had their employment not been interrupted by that service (the position they are qualified to perform); if their service lasted more than 90 days, that same rule applies, or a position of like seniority, status, and pay. Courts and the Department of Labor refer to this as the "escalator principle": Jordan Lee's reemployment position accounts for the seniority, status, and pay Jordan Lee would reasonably have attained by continuing to work through the period of service, not merely a return to the pre-service job.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(1) Except as provided in paragraphs (3) and (4), in the case of a person whose period of service in the uniformed services was for less than 91 days— (A) in the position of employment in which the person would have been employed if the continuous employment of such person with the employer had not been interrupted by such service, the duties of which the person is qualified to perform; or (B) in the position of employment in which the person was employed on the date of the commencement of the service in the uniformed services , only if the person is not qualified to perform the duties of the position referred to in subparagraph (A) after reasonable efforts by the employer to qualify the person. (2) Except as provided in paragraphs (3) and (4), in the case of a person whose period of service in the uniformed services was for more than 90 days— (A) in the position of employment in which the person would have been employed if the continuous employment of such person with the employer had not been interrupted by such service, or a position of like seniority , status and pay, the duties of which the person is qualified to perform"
  — 38 U.S.C. § 4313(a)(1)-(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, USERRA reemployment positions (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/38/4313)
  Known gap: The specific position-determination rule this clause describes covers the two most common service-length tiers. The statute sets out additional, more specific rules for a person who becomes disabled during service and cannot perform the escalator position even with reasonable accommodation, and separate rules apply to reemployment by the federal government. This document doesn't determine which tier or exception applies to a specific period of service.

PROTECTION AGAINST DISCHARGE AFTER REEMPLOYMENT
Once Jordan Lee is reemployed by Acme, Inc. under USERRA, Jordan Lee may not be discharged from that job except for cause for a period set by the length of the service that preceded reemployment: one year after the date of reemployment if that period of service was more than 180 days, or 180 days after the date of reemployment if that period of service was more than 30 days but less than 181 days.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A person who is reemployed by an employer under this chapter shall not be discharged from such employment, except for cause— (1) within one year after the date of such reemployment, if the person’s period of service before the reemployment was more than 180 days; or (2) within 180 days after the date of such reemployment, if the person’s period of service before the reemployment was more than 30 days but less than 181 days."
  — 38 U.S.C. § 4316(c) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, USERRA discharge protection after reemployment (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/38/4316)
  Known gap: The statute ties this heightened for-cause protection to two specific service-length tiers — more than 180 days, and more than 30 but fewer than 181 days — and doesn't itself set a separate heightened protection period for service of 30 days or less. "For cause" is not defined by this clause; USERRA and its implementing regulations address what counts as cause elsewhere. This document doesn't determine which tier applies to a specific reemployment or whether a specific discharge decision was actually for cause.

NON-DISCRIMINATION AND ANTI-RETALIATION
USERRA prohibits Acme, Inc. from denying Jordan Lee initial employment, reemployment, retention in employment, promotion, or any benefit of employment because of Jordan Lee's membership, application for membership, performance of service, application to perform service, or obligation to perform service in a uniformed service. Separately, an employer may not discriminate or retaliate against a person because that person has taken action to enforce a USERRA protection, testified or made a statement in a USERRA proceeding, assisted or participated in a USERRA investigation, or exercised a right under USERRA — and this anti-retaliation protection applies whether or not the person has ever served in the uniformed services.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A person who is a member of, applies to be a member of, performs, has performed, applies to perform, or has an obligation to perform service in a uniformed service shall not be denied initial employment, reemployment, retention in employment, promotion, or any benefit of employment by an employer on the basis of that membership, application for membership, performance of service, application for service, or obligation."
  — 38 U.S.C. § 4311(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, USERRA discrimination prohibition (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/38/4311)
  "An employer may not discriminate in employment against or take any adverse employment action or other retaliatory action against any person because such person (1) has taken an action to enforce a protection afforded any person under this chapter, (2) has testified or otherwise made a statement in or in connection with any proceeding under this chapter, (3) has assisted or otherwise participated in an investigation under this chapter, or (4) has exercised a right provided for in this chapter. The prohibition in this subsection shall apply with respect to a person regardless of whether that person has performed service in the uniformed services ."
  — 38 U.S.C. § 4311(b) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, USERRA anti-retaliation protection (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/38/4311)
  Known gap: Under the statute, a violation of the membership/service-basis rule is established if that status was a "motivating factor" in the employer's action, unless the employer proves it would have taken the same action anyway — this document doesn't apply that burden-shifting standard to any specific decision or determine whether service was in fact a motivating factor here.

CONTINUATION OF HEALTH PLAN COVERAGE DURING SERVICE
If Jordan Lee (or Jordan Lee's dependents) has coverage under Acme, Inc.'s health plan in connection with Jordan Lee's job, USERRA lets Jordan Lee elect to continue that coverage during the period of absence for uniformed service. The maximum period of continued coverage under that election is the lesser of the 24-month period beginning when the absence begins, or the day after Jordan Lee fails to apply for or return to a position of employment within USERRA's applicable time limits. A person who elects continued coverage may be required to pay up to 102% of the full premium, except that a person who serves less than 31 days may not be charged more than the employee's normal share, if any.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The maximum period of coverage of a person and the person’s dependents under such an election shall be the lesser of— (A) the 24-month period beginning on the date on which the person’s absence begins; or (B) the day after the date on which the person fails to apply for or return to a position of employment, as determined under section 4312(e). (2) A person who elects to continue health-plan coverage under this paragraph may be required to pay not more than 102 percent of the full premium under the plan (determined in the same manner as the applicable premium under section 4980B(f)(4) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 ) associated with such coverage for the employer’s other employees, except that in the case of a person who performs service in the uniformed services for less than 31 days, such person may not be required to pay more than the employee share, if any, for such coverage."
  — 38 U.S.C. § 4317(a)(1)-(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, USERRA health plan continuation (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/38/4317)
  Known gap: This describes the maximum continuation period and premium cap set by the statute itself; it doesn't state every rule governing multiemployer health plans or how liability for continued coverage is allocated between employers and plans in that setting, which the statute addresses separately.

HOW USERRA IS ENFORCED
A person who believes their USERRA rights have been violated may file a written complaint with the Secretary of Labor, who investigates it through the Department of Labor's Veterans' Employment and Training Service (VETS). If that effort to resolve the complaint against a state or private employer is unsuccessful, the person may ask the Secretary to refer the complaint to the U.S. Attorney General, who may choose to represent the person and sue on their behalf. Separately, a person may bring their own private lawsuit for USERRA relief against a state or private employer — without going through the Secretary or Attorney General at all, or after declining referral to the Attorney General, or after being refused representation by the Attorney General.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The Secretary (through the Veterans’ Employment and Training Service) shall provide assistance to any person with respect to the employment and reemployment rights and benefits to which such person is entitled under this chapter."
  — 38 U.S.C. § 4321 (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, USERRA reemployment assistance through VETS (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/38/4321)
  "A person who receives from the Secretary a notification pursuant to section 4322(e) of this title of an unsuccessful effort to resolve a complaint relating to a State (as an employer) or a private employer may request that the Secretary refer the complaint to the Attorney General. Not later than 60 days after the Secretary receives such a request with respect to a complaint, the Secretary shall refer the complaint to the Attorney General. If the Attorney General is reasonably satisfied that the person on whose behalf the complaint is referred is entitled to the rights or benefits sought, the Attorney General may appear on behalf of, and act as attorney for, the person on whose behalf the complaint is submitted and commence an action for relief under this chapter for such person."
  — 38 U.S.C. § 4323(a)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, USERRA referral to the Attorney General and private right of action (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/38/4323)
  "A person may commence an action for relief with respect to a complaint against a State (as an employer) or a private employer if the person— (A) has chosen not to apply to the Secretary for assistance under section 4322(a) of this title ; (B) has chosen not to request that the Secretary refer the complaint to the Attorney General under paragraph (1); or (C) has been refused representation by the Attorney General with respect to the complaint under such paragraph."
  — 38 U.S.C. § 4323(a)(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, USERRA private right of action (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/38/4323)
  Known gap: This describes the enforcement path for complaints against a state (as employer) or a private employer. USERRA sets out a separate enforcement mechanism, not described here, for complaints against the federal government as employer or against the Office of Personnel Management. This document doesn't evaluate the merits of any particular complaint.

USERRA INFORMATION ACKNOWLEDGMENT AND SIGNATURE
The information above is provided by Jordan Lee to Acme, Inc. in connection with a period of uniformed service and possible reemployment under USERRA.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Signature: _______________________________________________
Date: October 1, 2026
